tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.
My sister's flat is larger than mine.
Of the three trails, this path is the worse.
The new bus stop is closer than the old one.
She sings more better than she did at the school concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This suitcase is more heavier than the one I packed last summer.**

"Heavier" already includes the comparative ending -er, so pairing it with "more" doubles the mark. Repair: drop "more" and write simply "heavier than the one I packed last summer." One comparative marker is enough for a clean two-item contrast.
**B) My sister's flat is larger than mine.**

One-syllable "large" correctly becomes "larger" before "than." This is the standard short-adjective pattern for comparing two flats, and nothing extra is needed.
**C) Of the three trails, this path is the worse.**

"worse" is the comparative (two items), but "of the three trails" ranks a group of three. Repair: use the superlative "the worst." Among three or more options, -est / worst / best is the form you want.
**D) The new bus stop is closer than the old one.**

"Close" is short, so "closer than" correctly compares the new stop with the old one. Two named places → comparative, not superlative.
**E) She sings more better than she did at the school concert.**

"better" is already the irregular comparative of "well/good," so "more better" doubles the mark. Repair: sing "better than she did at the school concert." Never stack "more" on an irregular comparative.
tasks.solution_overview:
Suitcases, flats, trails, bus stops, and a school concert — everyday scenes asking whether each comparison is marked correctly.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This opener targets double marking and the two-versus-many rule. Short adjectives usually take -er / -est; irregulars like better and worse already carry the comparative meaning, so stacking "more" on top is always wrong.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For each line, ask two questions: Is the adjective already comparative or superlative? And does the sentence compare two things or rank a whole group? Mark true only when both the form and the grade of comparison fit.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.
That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.
The evening train was quieter than the morning service.
This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.
It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Among the five bakeries on the high street, Miller's has the freshest bread.**

Five bakeries on the high street is a clear group, and "the freshest" correctly ranks Miller's inside that set. Superlative -est fits one-syllable "fresh" without needing "most."
**B) That soup tastes gooder than the one from yesterday.**

English never forms "gooder." The irregular chain is good → better → best. Repair: "That soup tastes better than the one from yesterday." Learn the irregular and refuse invented -er forms.
**C) The evening train was quieter than the morning service.**

Two-syllable "quiet" commonly takes -er: "quieter than the morning service" cleanly contrasts two trains. No need for "more quiet" here.
**D) This novel is more interesting than the film adaptation.**

Multi-syllable "interesting" correctly takes "more … than" when the novel is set against the film. Longer adjectives almost never add -er.
**E) It was the most coldest winter walk we have ever taken.**

"coldest" is already the superlative, so "most coldest" doubles it. Repair: "the coldest winter walk we have ever taken." Pair "most" only with the base adjective, never with -est.
tasks.solution_overview:
Bakeries, soup, trains, a novel-versus-film pair, and a winter walk — check that each adjective picks the right comparative system.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

You are sorting -er/-est against more/most, spotting mangled irregulars such as "gooder," and catching double superlatives like "most coldest." Longer adjectives prefer more/most; short ones usually take the ending.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the adjective, count its syllables, and ask whether the sentence ranks inside a group. If you see "most" glued to an -est form, or a homemade -er on an irregular, mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is more taller than his twin brother.
Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.
Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.
The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.
My laptop runs gooder after the software update.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He is more taller than his twin brother.**

"taller" already carries -er, so "more taller" is double marking. Repair: "He is taller than his twin brother." Delete "more" whenever -er is already present.
**B) Of all the desserts, this tart is the less sweet.**

"of all the desserts" ranks a whole set, so you need the superlative "the least sweet," not comparative "the less sweet." Less compares two; least ranks many.
**C) Her explanation was clearer than the textbook chapter.**

Two-syllable "clear" commonly forms "clearer than" for a textbook contrast. The comparative ending is natural here and needs no repair.
**D) The weekend weather turned more worser after noon.**

"worse" is already comparative, and "worser" is nonstandard — "more worser" piles both errors. Repair: "turned worse after noon." Remember bad → worse → worst with no extras.
**E) My laptop runs gooder after the software update.**

"gooder" is not English. Repair: "My laptop runs better after the software update." Keep the fixed chain good / better / best.
tasks.solution_overview:
Twins, desserts, a textbook chapter, worsening weather, and a laptop update — a dense run of beginner comparison traps.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set stacks double marking ("more taller," "more worser"), less versus least, and broken irregulars ("gooder"). Fix the comparison word itself before you worry about style.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

First strip any stacked "more" or invented -er. Then check whether "of all" demands a superlative (least, not less). Irregulars bad/good have fixed shapes — do not reinvent them.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.
She chose the most cheap ticket available online.
Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.
This playlist is the best of the three we built.
The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Today's quiz was easier than Monday's.**

"Easy" correctly changes y to i and adds -er: "easier than Monday's." The spelling shift is standard for consonant + y adjectives in two-item contrasts.
**B) She chose the most cheap ticket available online.**

one-syllable "cheap" wants "the cheapest ticket," not "the most cheap." Repair: swap to -est. Prefer the ending on short adjectives unless the -est form sounds awkward.
**C) Our garden is smaller than the neighbour's.**

"Small" simply adds -er: "smaller than the neighbour's" is the standard comparative. No consonant doubling is required here (unlike big → bigger).
**D) This playlist is the best of the three we built.**

"The best of the three" correctly uses the irregular superlative inside a set of three playlists. Good → better → best fits the group ranking.
**E) The museum was more farther from the hotel than we expected.**

"farther/further" is already comparative, so "more farther" doubles the mark. Repair: "farther/further from the hotel than we expected." Irregular distance forms never take an extra "more."
tasks.solution_overview:
A quiz, online tickets, neighbouring gardens, playlists, and a museum walk — spelling and irregular distance forms come into play.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Confirm -er spelling (easy → easier), avoid "most" on short adjectives that want -est, and leave irregulars like best and farther alone. They do not need an extra "more."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the ending first, then the intensifier or "most." If the adjective is already comparative or irregular, strip any stacked marker before you tick true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.
Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.
She felt worse after skipping breakfast.
Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.
His second attempt was better than the first.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This curry is spicier than the mild version on the menu.**

"Spicy" forms "spicier" for a clean two-item food contrast with the mild menu option. The -y → -ier change is standard and needs no "more."
**B) Between the two coats, the wool one is the warmest.**

only two coats are in play, so the superlative "the warmest" overshoots. Repair: "the wool one is warmer." Between two → comparative; among many → superlative.
**C) She felt worse after skipping breakfast.**

"Worse" is the correct irregular comparative of bad/ill after skipping breakfast. No "more" and no "worser" — the form stands alone.
**D) Of the four rooms, the attic is the more quiet.**

four rooms need a superlative, but "the more quiet" is only comparative. Repair: "the quietest" (or "the most quiet"). Groups of three or more take the highest grade.
**E) His second attempt was better than the first.**

"Better than the first" correctly compares two attempts with the irregular comparative. Two items → better; a whole group → best.
tasks.solution_overview:
Curry heat, two coats, skipped breakfast, four rooms, and two exam attempts — the two-versus-many rule is the headline.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Focus on whether the cue phrase compares a pair or ranks a group. "Between the two" almost always wants a comparative; "of the four" wants a superlative. Keep irregular worse/better clean.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Circle the quantity words (between two, of four, than the first). Match comparative to pairs and superlative to groups of three or more, then confirm irregular spelling.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.
This café is more popular than the one by the river.
My phone battery lasts longer than yours.
She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.
He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The kitchen looked tidier after we cleared the counter.**

"Tidy" correctly becomes "tidier" after clearing the counter. Consonant + y → -ier is the expected spelling for this short adjective.
**B) This café is more popular than the one by the river.**

Three-syllable "popular" correctly takes "more … than" against the riverside café. Long adjectives almost always use more/most rather than -er/-est.
**C) My phone battery lasts longer than yours.**

"Longer than yours" cleanly compares battery life for two phones. Duration often rides on long / longer / longest without needing "more."
**D) She bought the least expensive bike in the shop.**

"The least expensive bike in the shop" correctly ranks cost among many options. Least + adjective is the standard superlative of inferiority.
**E) He runs more faster in the evenings than in the mornings.**

"faster" already marks the comparative, so "more faster" doubles it. Repair: "He runs faster in the evenings than in the mornings." -er adverbs reject an extra "more" just as adjectives do.
tasks.solution_overview:
A tidier kitchen, café popularity, phone batteries, bike prices, and evening runs — mostly clean models with one stacked adverb trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Most lines show healthy -ier, more + long adjective, -er for duration, and least + adjective for ranking cost. The clear fault is stacking "more" on an -er adverb such as "faster."

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat the first four as reference forms. On the last, strip the extra "more" so only one comparative marker remains before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The river is deeper here than near the bridge.
Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.
Their dog is friendlier than ours.
She felt more happier after the phone call.
This is the worst film I have seen all year.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The river is deeper here than near the bridge.**

"Deeper than near the bridge" correctly compares two stretches of the same river. One-syllable adjectives take -er for two-item contrasts.
**B) Of the two recipes, this one is the simplest.**

only two recipes are named, so "the simplest" is the wrong grade. Repair: "this one is simpler." Of/between two → comparative, not superlative.
**C) Their dog is friendlier than ours.**

"Friendly" correctly forms "friendlier" ("more friendly" is also acceptable). The -y → -ier pattern is natural for this personality comparison.
**D) She felt more happier after the phone call.**

"happier" already includes the comparative, so "more happier" doubles the mark. Repair: "She felt happier after the phone call." Remember happy → happier → happiest.
**E) This is the worst film I have seen all year.**

"The worst film I have seen all year" correctly uses the irregular superlative for a broad ranking. Bad → worse → worst needs no extras.
tasks.solution_overview:
River depth, two recipes, friendly dogs, a happy phone call, and a miserable film — watch "of the two" especially.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

"Of the two" almost always blocks a superlative. Keep -ier spelling tidy on friendlier/happier, and leave irregular worst alone once the grade of comparison is right.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the cue says two, demand a comparative. If the cue ranks a year of films or a clear group, allow the superlative. Then check for stacked "more" on -ier forms.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.
He is the elder of the two cousins.
This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.
Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.
We walked further than planned before turning back.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The second episode was less exciting than the pilot.**

"Less exciting than the pilot" correctly softens a longer adjective across two episodes. Less + adjective + than is the comparative of inferiority.
**B) He is the elder of the two cousins.**

"The elder of the two cousins" is a traditional family comparative for people in a pair. Elder/eldest mainly for family; older/oldest for general age — both patterns are known in exams.
**C) This rucksack is bigest than I need for a day hike.**

spelling and grade both fail — "bigest than" should be "bigger than." Repair: double the g and use comparative with than: big → bigger → biggest.
**D) Among her hobbies, pottery is the most relaxing.**

"The most relaxing" correctly ranks pottery among several hobbies. -ing adjectives of three syllables take most, not -est.
**E) We walked further than planned before turning back.**

"Further than planned" is a standard irregular comparative of distance/extent. Farther/further both work for physical distance in modern English.
tasks.solution_overview:
TV episodes, cousins, a day-hike rucksack, hobbies, and an overlong walk — less + adjective, family elder, and the big/bigger spelling trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set adds comparative of inferiority (less + adjective), the family form elder, and the spelling trap big → bigger (not "bigest"). Read than-clauses carefully: they want a comparative, not a mangled superlative.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check the preposition and ending on each line. Than + misspelled -est is an automatic false; less + long adjective + than is usually fine.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.
Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.
The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.
He is not as tall as his older sister.
The sequel was as good than the original.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This tea is as strong as the one from the market stall.**

"As strong as the one from the market stall" correctly states equal strength. As … as compares sameness, not ranking, and both markers are present.
**B) Her handwriting is as neat than her brother's.**

** than belongs with comparatives; as … as marks equality.

Trap: after "as neat" you need "as," not "than." Repair: "as neat as her brother's." Than belongs with comparatives; as … as marks equality.
**C) The park feels as peaceful as it did in spring.**

"As peaceful as it did in spring" correctly keeps both as-markers for equal calm. Dropping the second as would break the pattern.
**D) He is not as tall as his older sister.**

"Not as tall as his older sister" is the standard negative equality pattern. In everyday meaning it is close to "less tall than," but the frame stays as … as.
**E) The sequel was as good than the original.**

** Never mix as … than.

Trap: "as good than" mixes the two systems. Repair: "as good as the original." Never write as … than.
tasks.solution_overview:
Tea strength, handwriting, a peaceful park, height in the family, and a film sequel — equality lives in the as … as frame.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Equality comparisons use as + adjective + as. If than sneaks in after as + adjective, the sentence is wrong — swap than for the second as. Negative equality (not as … as) is still the same frame.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for both as-markers. A lone as before the adjective with than after it is the classic trap; rebuild as … as before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She drives much more carefully than she did last year.
This bag is far heavier than it looks.
The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.
He speaks English better than I expected.
They arrived slightly earlier than the others.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She drives much more carefully than she did last year.**

"Much more carefully" correctly strengthens the comparative of a -ly adverb. Much / far / a lot can boost a single comparative without changing its form.
**B) This bag is far heavier than it looks.**

"Far heavier" correctly intensifies a short -er comparative. Far + -er is natural and strong for surprise weight.
**C) The climb was a lot more harder than the map suggested.**

** Intensifiers sit before one comparative form, not two.

Trap: "a lot more harder" doubles the comparative. Repair: "a lot harder" or "much harder." Intensifiers sit before one comparative form, not two.
**D) He speaks English better than I expected.**

"Better than I expected" correctly compares performance with the irregular comparative; the clause after than is fine. Better needs no "more."
**E) They arrived slightly earlier than the others.**

"Slightly earlier" correctly softens the comparative of "early." Slightly / a bit / rather can modify comparatives without adding a second marker.
tasks.solution_overview:
Careful driving, a deceptively heavy bag, a hard climb, better English, and an early arrival — intensifiers meet single comparative forms.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Intensifiers such as much, far, a lot, and slightly are fine before one comparative. They become wrong the moment they sit beside a second marker such as more + -er.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Allow the booster only if exactly one comparative remains. If you see "a lot more harder," strip either "more" or the -er ending — never keep both.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.
She is one of the smarter students in the class.
This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.
He is one of the tallest player on the team.
That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Prague is one of the most beautiful cities I have visited.**

"One of the most beautiful cities I have visited" hits all three slots: superlative, plural cities, and the "one of the" frame. This is the model pattern.
**B) She is one of the smarter students in the class.**

** one of the blocks ordinary comparatives.

Trap: after "one of the" you need a superlative, not comparative "smarter." Repair: "one of the smartest students in the class." The frame blocks ordinary comparatives.
**C) This is one of the best meals we have cooked at home.**

"One of the best meals" correctly pairs the irregular superlative with a plural noun. Best / worst fit the same frame as most + adjective.
**D) He is one of the tallest player on the team.**

** one of + plural always.

Trap: "one of" requires a plural noun, but "player" is singular. Repair: "one of the tallest players on the team." Always plural after one of.
**E) That was one of the funnier jokes in the show.**

** Comparative -er forms do not follow "one of the."

Trap: "funnier" is comparative, but the frame wants a superlative. Repair: "one of the funniest jokes in the show." Comparative -er forms do not follow "one of the."
highlights: one of the most beautiful cities
tasks.solution_overview:
Cities, classmates, home-cooked meals, teammates, and jokes — the fixed frame one of the + superlative + plural noun.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Remember the package: one of the + superlative + plural noun. Ordinary comparatives and singular nouns after "one of" are the usual exam traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check three slots every time: "one of the," a true superlative (not -er), and a plural noun. Fail any slot and mark false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The more she practised, the more confident she became.
The harder he trained, the better his times got.
More she waited, more anxious she felt.
The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.
The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The more she practised, the more confident she became.**

"The more she practised, the more confident she became" correctly links two parallel comparatives. Keep "the" before each comparative in this pattern.
**B) The harder he trained, the better his times got.**

"The harder he trained, the better his times got" shows that -er and irregular comparatives both fit the frame. The pairing is grammatical and natural.
**C) More she waited, more anxious she felt.**

** Dropping "the" breaks the correlative comparative.

Trap: both articles are missing. Repair: "The more she waited, the more anxious she felt." Dropping "the" breaks the correlative comparative.
**D) The less we argued, the happier the evening felt.**

"The less we argued, the happier the evening felt" is a valid inferiority pair. Less / fewer can lead the first half without trouble.
**E) The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be.**

"The sooner you book, the cheaper the tickets will be" is a classic fixed double comparative pairing time with cost. Both halves keep "the" + comparative.
tasks.solution_overview:
Practice and confidence, training and times, waiting and anxiety, fewer arguments, early booking — correlative the … the … pairs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Correlative comparatives need "the + comparative" in both halves. Mixed shapes (harder / better, less / happier, sooner / cheaper) are fine; missing "the" is not.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Read left and right of the comma. If either article "the" disappears before a comparative, rebuild the correlative before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.
He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.
Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.
The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.
They danced more graceful than the other couple.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She paints more skilfully than anyone else in the club.**

"More skilfully" correctly forms the comparative of a -ly adverb for how she paints. Long adverbs take more/most, not -er.
**B) He finished the puzzle quicker than I did.**

"Quicker" (or "more quickly") is acceptable in modern usage for manner here. Short adverb comparatives often allow -er in everyday English when finishing a puzzle.
**C) Please speak more slow so I can follow the recipe.**

** Adjective slow ≠ adverb slowly.

Trap: "more slow" uses the adjective where the verb speak needs an adverb. Repair: "Please speak more slowly so I can follow the recipe." Adjective slow ≠ adverb slowly.
**D) The choir sang better last night than at the rehearsal.**

"Better" correctly compares how the choir sang on two occasions. The adverb chain is well → better → best.
**E) They danced more graceful than the other couple.**

** After danced/spoke/sang, prefer adverb forms.

Trap: manner after danced needs "more gracefully," not the adjective "graceful." Repair: "They danced more gracefully than the other couple." Prefer adverb forms after danced/spoke/sang.
tasks.solution_overview:
Painting, puzzles, recipe instructions, choir night, and a dance floor — separate adjective comparison from adverb comparison.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

When the word modifies a verb (speak, dance, sing), you usually need an adverb comparative — more slowly / more gracefully / better — not a bare adjective. Long -ly adverbs take more/most.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask what is being compared: a person/thing or a manner of action. Manner after a verb almost always wants an adverb form; mark false when an adjective leaks into that slot.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.
Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.
Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.
The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.
His answer was different from mine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) This jacket is superior than the one I bought last winter.**

** superior / inferior / preferable → to.

Trap: Latinate "superior" pairs with "to," not "than." Repair: "superior to the one I bought last winter." Superior / inferior / preferable → to.
**B) Her design is inferior to the earlier sketch.**

"Inferior to the earlier sketch" is the correct fixed comparative-like pattern. Do not rewrite these with homemade -er forms.
**C) Fresh pasta is preferable to the dried kind for this sauce.**

"Preferable to the dried kind" correctly states a preference between two pasta options. Preferable to ≈ better as a choice than, but the preposition stays "to."
**D) The coastal path is preferable than the inland route.**

** Preferable never takes than.

Trap: preferable never takes than. Repair: "preferable to the inland route." Swap than for to and keep the rest.
**E) His answer was different from mine.**

"Different from mine" is the standard British exam form. Treat different from as the safe choice in tested writing.
tasks.solution_overview:
Jackets, sketches, pasta, coastal paths, and different answers — Latinate comparison words that lock to fixed prepositions.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Some comparison words never take than. Superior, inferior, and preferable lock to "to." Learn those fixed prepositions separately from ordinary -er / more patterns. Different from is the safe exam form.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When you see superior/inferior/preferable, demand "to." Than after those adjectives is an automatic false; ordinary -er comparatives still use than as usual.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.
We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.
She made less mistakes on the second draft.
He drinks less coffee than he used to.
There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.
tactical_explanations:
**A) There were fewer people at the market than on Saturday.**

"Fewer people" correctly uses fewer with a countable plural at the market. Fewer + countable; less + uncountable is the core split.
**B) We had less time than we needed to catch the ferry.**

"Less time" correctly pairs with uncountable time before the ferry. Time, money, traffic, and advice usually take less.
**C) She made less mistakes on the second draft.**

** If you can count them, prefer fewer in careful English.

Trap: "mistakes" is countable, so "less mistakes" is wrong in careful English. Repair: "fewer mistakes on the second draft." If you can count them, prefer fewer.
**D) He drinks less coffee than he used to.**

"Less coffee" correctly treats coffee as an uncountable amount. Less + mass noun is the natural pairing for drinks measured as volume.
**E) There is fewer traffic on this road after nine.**

** fewer needs a plural countable noun.

Trap: "traffic" is uncountable, so "fewer traffic" fails. Repair: "less traffic on this road after nine." Fewer needs a plural countable noun.
tasks.solution_overview:
Market crowds, ferry clocks, draft mistakes, coffee habits, and road traffic — less versus fewer by noun type.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Less and fewer are comparative quantity words. Decide first whether the noun is countable plural or an uncountable mass, then pick fewer or less.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If you can count separate units (people, mistakes), prefer fewer. If you measure a mass (time, coffee, traffic), use less. That single test decides most of A–E.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.
The music grew more and more louder near the stage.
The waves became higher and higher before the storm.
She felt worse and worse during the long flight.
The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.
tactical_explanations:
**A) My week got busier and busier as the festival approached.**

"Busier and busier" correctly shows gradual increase with a repeated comparative as the festival nears. Adj-er and adj-er = steadily more.
**B) The music grew more and more louder near the stage.**

** Pick one comparative system and stick to it.

Trap: "more and more louder" doubles the marking. Repair: "louder and louder" or "more and more loud." Pick one comparative system and stick to it.
**C) The waves became higher and higher before the storm.**

"Higher and higher" correctly intensifies a short comparative as the waves build. Repeat the -er form for gradual change.
**D) She felt worse and worse during the long flight.**

"Worse and worse" correctly repeats the irregular comparative on the long flight. Irregulars can double the same way: better and better, worse and worse.
**E) The puzzle grew increasingly more difficult toward the end.**

** Do not stack increasingly with more.

Trap: "increasingly" already means "more and more," so "increasingly more difficult" is redundant. Repair: "increasingly difficult" or "more and more difficult." Do not stack increasingly with more.
tasks.solution_overview:
A busy festival week, stage volume, rising waves, a long flight, and a toughening puzzle — gradual-change patterns.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Gradual change either repeats one comparative (louder and louder) or uses more and more + base adjective. Mixing systems — or adding increasingly to more — creates double marking.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Pick one system and stick to it. If you see "more and more" beside an -er form, or "increasingly more," strip the redundancy before marking true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.
This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.
She is taller than any girl in her class.
This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.
He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.
tactical_explanations:
**A) No other beach on the island is as clean as this one.**

"No other beach on the island is as clean as this one" correctly sets up a unique equality comparison. No other + as … as ≈ this is the cleanest.
**B) This hostel is cheaper than any other place we checked.**

"Cheaper than any other place we checked" correctly excludes the rest of the set. Any other keeps the compared hostel outside the group.
**C) She is taller than any girl in her class.**

** Without other/else, the sentence oddly includes her in "any girl."

Trap: without other/else, she remains inside "any girl in her class." Repair: "taller than any other girl" (or "anyone else"). Exclusion words prevent logical self-comparison.
**D) This route is the shortest of any other path to the lake.**

** Superlative and "any other" usually fight each other.

Trap: do not mix "the shortest" with "of any other." Repair: "the shortest path" or "shorter than any other path to the lake." Superlative and "any other" usually fight each other.
**E) He plays the piano better than anyone else in the family.**

"Better than anyone else in the family" correctly uses else to exclude him from the comparison group. Else / other prevents logical self-comparison.
tasks.solution_overview:
Island beaches, hostels, classroom height, lake paths, and family piano — advanced comparison hinges on exclusion words.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Other and else keep the compared person or thing outside the group. Without them, someone can be compared with a set that still includes that person — a classic logic trap. Superlative plus "any other" usually fights itself.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check whether the compared item is excluded. Add other/else when needed, and do not glue "the shortest" to "of any other" in the same breath.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.
She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.
They would rather stay in than go out tonight.
He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.
We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I prefer walking to cycling when the weather is mild.**

"Prefer walking to cycling" is the standard comparative preference pattern with parallel gerunds. Prefer + noun/gerund + to + noun/gerund.
**B) She prefers tea than coffee in the morning.**

** prefer … than is almost always wrong.

Trap: prefer takes "to," not "than." Repair: "prefers tea to coffee in the morning." Prefer … than is almost always wrong.
**C) They would rather stay in than go out tonight.**

"Would rather stay in than go out tonight" correctly contrasts two base-verb options. Would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive.
**D) He would rather to leave early than miss the last train.**

** Delete to after would rather.

Trap: after "would rather" use the bare infinitive, not "to leave." Repair: "would rather leave early than miss the last train." Delete to after would rather.
**E) We prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway.**

"Prefer cooking at home rather than ordering takeaway" is an accepted alternative with parallel -ing forms. Keep the two sides parallel (cooking / ordering).
tasks.solution_overview:
Walking versus cycling, tea versus coffee, stay-in versus go-out, early trains, and home cooking — preference structures as cousins of comparatives.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Preference patterns are prefer A to B, and would rather A than B. Watch the preposition (to, not than after prefer) and the bare infinitive after would rather (no "to").

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the structure first. Prefer wants to; would rather wants than plus a base verb. Parallel -ing forms keep prefer … rather than … tidy.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.
This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.
Her second cake was twice as large as the first.
The second half was half as long than the opening act.
Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The new café is nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be.**

"Nowhere near as busy as the old one used to be" correctly intensifies a negative equality comparison. Nowhere near as / not nearly as + adjective + as.
**B) This trail is not nearly as steep than the guidebook claimed.**

** Intensifiers do not change the need for a second as.

Trap: keep the as … as frame — "not nearly as steep as the guidebook claimed," not "than." Intensifiers do not cancel the need for a second as.
**C) Her second cake was twice as large as the first.**

"Twice as large as the first" correctly multiplies an equality comparison. Twice / three times + as + adjective + as is the fixed scale pattern.
**D) The second half was half as long than the opening act.**

** Multipliers still need as … as.

Trap: write "half as long as," not "half as long than." Multipliers still need as … as even when the idea is reduction.
**E) Today feels slightly less humid than yesterday.**

"Slightly less humid than yesterday" correctly softens a comparative of inferiority. Less + adjective + than remains available beside as … as patterns.
tasks.solution_overview:
Busy cafés, steep trails, oversized cakes, show lengths, and humidity — scaled equality still needs a closing as.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Scaled equality (twice as, half as, not nearly as, nowhere near as) still needs a closing as. Than only returns when you switch to a true comparative such as less … than.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

If the line opens with twice/half/not nearly/nowhere near + as, demand a matching as later. Replace any than in that slot before you mark true.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.
She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.
This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.
He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.
That was by far a better concert than the one in March.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit.**

"Of all the local markets, this one sells the freshest fruit" correctly pairs a group phrase with a superlative. Of all / among all → superlative.
**B) She is by far the most organised person in our flatshare.**

"By far the most organised person in our flatshare" correctly intensifies a superlative. By far / easily / much the + superlative is the usual package.
**C) This crossword is much the harder I have tried this month.**

** much the + -est / most …

Trap: with "much the," use a superlative — "much the hardest," not "much the harder." Repair the grade: much the + -est / most …
**D) He is easily the funniest host on the late-night shows.**

"Easily the funniest host on the late-night shows" correctly strengthens a superlative ranking. Easily the + superlative is common in speech and exams.
**E) That was by far a better concert than the one in March.**

"By far a better concert than the one in March" can intensify a comparative when exactly two concerts are compared. By far works with both superlatives and clear two-item comparatives.
tasks.solution_overview:
Local markets, organised flatmates, tough crosswords, late-night hosts, and concerts — intensifiers locked onto the right grade of comparison.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Final polish: intensifiers like by far, easily, and much the usually lock onto superlatives. If the sentence clearly compares only two items, a comparative after by far can still work — but "much the harder" is the wrong grade.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match the booster to the comparison grade. Of all / among → superlative; a clear pair after by far may keep a comparative. Reject "much the" + comparative.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE
